To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the likelihood of participation, and the intensity of participation, in non violent and violent political action is a function of socioeconomic status, with non violent participation highest among the upper and lower middle classes, and violent participation highest among those who fall in the middle.

(1) political action is a continuum from non-violent to violent activities, (2) political violence is a credible alternative to non-violent protest for individuals for whom non violent protest carries little signaling content, and (3) the likelihood of political engagement is highest in the middle of the income distribution, with support for violent action concentrated among the lower-middle class.

(i) the likelihood of participation increases with income, but (ii) there is a non linear relationship between socioeconomic status and the likelihood of participation, and (iii) the likelihood of violent participation is highest among lower middle class individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the political behavior of citizens across the Arab world and the role that socioeconomic status plays in shaping that behavior.
the question of why political participation varies in the Arab world and we show that it is a function of the cost of signaling discontent.
the question of how the political behavior of individuals in the Arab world is shaped by the costs and benefits of political participation and the nature of the regime.

the lower middle class is the most likely group to be engaged in political activity, and this group is more likely to engage in political violence than any other group in the Arab world.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
political behavior in the region is best understood in terms of signaling discontent.
political participation in the Arab world is not only a function of economic status, but also of the cost of political engagement.
socioeconomic status is an important determinant of political behavior in the Arab world, but that the effect of socioeconomic status is not linear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the political landscape of the Arab world in the wake of the Arab Spring is one of considerable diversity and nuance.

the Arab Spring was not a spontaneous outpouring of anger but rather the product of years of political mobilization by the middle classes, a group that has historically been underrepresented in the political process.

the Arab world is not a monolithic bloc, and that political behavior in the region cannot be understood without reference to the socioeconomic characteristics of those who participate in political action.
